title: Money Fundamentals
description: Where money comes from, where it goes, and how to read the paperwork.
wolfLine: Broke is a habit. So is rich. Pick one.

income.definition: Money that comes in to you.
income.example: The pay from your job, or money from selling something you own.

expense.definition: Money that goes out of your pocket to pay for something.
expense.example: Rent, groceries, a bus ticket, a phone bill.

cash-flow.definition: What's left after you take your expenses away from your income.
cash-flow.example: Earn $2,000 a month, spend $1,500, and your cash flow is $500.

gross-pay.definition: What you earned before anything is taken out.
gross-pay.example: 80 hours at $17.50 an hour is $1,400 gross pay.

deduction.definition: Money taken out of your pay before you get it, like taxes or retirement savings.
deduction.example: Federal income tax and Social Security are deductions.

take-home-pay.definition: What actually lands in your bank account after every deduction. Also called net pay.
take-home-pay.example: $1,400 gross pay minus $320.60 of deductions is $1,079.40 take-home pay.

fixed-expense.definition: An expense that costs the same amount every month.
fixed-expense.example: Rent, or a phone plan with a set monthly price.

variable-expense.definition: An expense that changes from month to month, depending on what you do.

need.definition: Something you have to pay for to live and work.
need.example: A place to live, basic food, getting to your job.

want.definition: Something that makes life nicer, but you'd be fine without.
want.example: Concert tickets, a new video game, takeout.

lifestyle-creep.definition: When you earn more and your spending quietly rises to match, so you don't end up any better off.
lifestyle-creep.example: You get a raise, then start eating out more until the raise is gone.

asset.definition: Something you own that's worth money.
asset.example: Money in the bank, a car, a laptop you could sell.

liability.definition: Money you owe to someone else.
liability.example: A car loan you're still paying off.

net-worth.definition: Everything you own minus everything you owe.
net-worth.example: Own $10,000, owe $4,000, and your net worth is $6,000.

due-date.definition: The last day you can pay a bill without it counting as late.
due-date.example: An electricity bill due Oct 21 must be paid by Oct 21.

late-fee.definition: An extra charge for paying a bill after its due date.
late-fee.example: Pay an $84 bill four days late and it becomes $99.

lessons.title: Money In, Money Out
lessons.summary: Where money comes from and where it goes.

steps.title: Start here
steps.body:
Money only ever does two things. It comes **in** to you, and it goes **out** from you.

That's it. Get a grip on both and you're already ahead of most people. No experience needed. We'll teach every word as we go.

steps.context: Money that comes **in** to you is called [[income]].
steps.prompt: Which of these is income?
choices: The pay you get from your job
steps.explain: Pay from a job is the most common kind of [[income]]. Selling something you own counts too.

steps.context: Money that goes **out** to pay for something is an [[expense]].
steps.prompt: Which of these is an expense?
choices: Money a friend pays you back
steps.explain: You pay for groceries, so money goes out. That's an [[expense]].

steps.prompt: The rent you pay each month is [[income]].
steps.explain: Rent is money going out, so it's an [[expense]].

steps.context: Take your expenses away from your income and you get your [[cash flow]]: what’s left over. Earn $2,000, spend $1,500, and your cash flow is $500.
steps.prompt: You earn $3,200 a month and spend $2,900. What’s your cash flow?
steps.explain: $3,200 − $2,900 = $300. That’s money you can save, or use to pay off what you owe.

steps.context: When income is bigger than expenses, cash flow is **positive**. When expenses are bigger, it's **negative**: you're spending money you don't have.
steps.prompt: You earn $1,800 a month but spend $2,000. Your cash flow is ___.
steps.explain: You’re $200 short every month. That gap has to come from savings or borrowing.

steps.prompt: Your [[cash flow]] is positive. What does that tell you?
choices: You spend more than you earn
You earn more than you spend
You have no expenses at all
steps.explain: Money left over every month. That's the goal.

steps.prompt: Recap: match each word to what it means.

lessons.title: Your First Paycheck
lessons.summary: Read a real pay stub: what you earned, what got taken, what you keep.

steps.context: Here’s your first pay stub from a coffee shop job. Your [[gross pay]] is everything you earned, before anything is taken out.
steps.prompt: How much did you earn for these two weeks, before anything came out?
why: That’s what’s left after deductions. Gross is before.
That’s the total taken out, not what you earned.
steps.explain: Gross pay is the top line: 80 hours × $17.50.

steps.context: Money taken out of your pay before you get it is a [[deduction]]. Taxes are deductions. So is money you choose to save for retirement.
steps.prompt: How much federal income tax came out of this paycheck?
steps.explain: Federal income tax: $112.00. It’s listed under Deductions.

steps.context: What’s left after every deduction is your [[take-home pay]], also called net pay. It’s the number that actually lands in your account.
steps.prompt: How much actually lands in your bank account?
why: That’s gross pay. Deductions come out first.
That only takes out the federal tax. Every deduction comes out.

steps.context: Not every deduction is a tax. Some of it is still your money, just saved for later.
steps.prompt: One deduction is you saving for retirement, not a tax. Tap it.
steps.explain: A 401(k) is a retirement account. That $56 is still yours, invested for later.

steps.prompt: You get paid twice a month, the same amount each time. What’s your take-home pay for the month?
steps.explain: $1,079.40 × 2 = $2,158.80. That’s the number to plan your month around, not $2,800.

steps.prompt: Your gross pay is the amount that lands in your bank account.
steps.explain: That’s [[take-home pay]]. Gross pay is before deductions.

steps.prompt: Taxes taken out of your paycheck are called ___.
steps.explain: They’re deducted before the money reaches you.

lessons.title: Fixed vs. Variable
lessons.summary: Which costs are locked in and which you control.

steps.context: Some [[expenses|expense]] cost exactly the same every month, like rent. Those are [[fixed expenses|fixed-expense]].
steps.prompt: Which of these is most likely a fixed expense?
steps.explain: Same rent, every month. Fixed.

steps.context: Other expenses go up and down depending on what you do, like food or fuel. Those are [[variable expenses|variable-expense]].
steps.prompt: Which of these is a variable expense?
choices: A phone plan that costs the same every month
steps.explain: Drive more, spend more. Drive less, spend less. Variable.

steps.prompt: Groceries are a [[fixed expense]].
steps.explain: Your grocery bill changes month to month, so it's a [[variable expense]].

steps.prompt: Match each word to what it means.

steps.context: Add both kinds together to get your total spending. Fixed $1,000 + variable $500 = $1,500 a month.
steps.prompt: Your fixed expenses are $1,200 a month and your variable expenses are $700. What do you spend in total?
You want to free up some money this month. Which is usually quickest to cut?
steps.explain: You can't change your rent tomorrow, but you can skip takeout tonight.

steps.prompt: A gym membership that costs the same every month is a ___ expense.
steps.explain: Same price every month, so it's fixed, even though you could cancel it.

steps.prompt: Sort these monthly costs.

steps.context: A [[need]] is something you have to pay for to live and work: a place to live, basic food, getting to your job.
steps.prompt: Which of these is a need?
steps.explain: You need somewhere to live. The rest is optional.

steps.context: A [[want]] is something that makes life nicer, but you'd be fine without it.
steps.prompt: Which of these is a want?
steps.explain: Fun, but you'd survive without it. That's a [[want]].

steps.prompt: Upgrading to the newest phone when yours still works fine is a [[need]].
steps.explain: A working phone is a need. The upgrade is a want.

steps.context: Careful: wants love to hide inside needs. Food is a need, but takeout every night is a want.
steps.prompt: You need a car to get to work, so you buy a brand-new one with leather seats and a premium sound system. Which part is the want?
choices: The leather seats and sound system
steps.explain: The car is the need. The extras are wants riding along.

steps.context: When people start earning more, they often spend more on wants without noticing. That's called [[lifestyle creep]].
steps.prompt: You got a raise six months ago, but you're not saving any more than before. What probably happened?
steps.explain: The extra money got spent on wants, a little at a time.

steps.prompt: You need to cut spending fast. Where do you look first?
steps.explain: Wants can go tomorrow without breaking anything.

steps.prompt: Need or want? Sort them.

steps.context: Groceries are a need. But a want can still sneak into the basket.
steps.prompt: Here’s this week’s grocery receipt. Tap the want.

doc.title: Fresh Market
doc.subtitle: Store #214 · Sat 10:42 AM
doc.note: Tax charged on non-food items only.

steps.explain: Four energy drinks a week is $11.96, or over $600 a year.

lessons.title: Jordan’s First Month
lessons.summary: Read about one real-feeling month, then work out where the money went.

story.title: Where did it all go?
story.body:
Jordan just moved into a first apartment and started a full-time job. Every month, **$2,400** of take-home pay lands in Jordan’s account.

Rent is **$1,100**. Phone and internet are **$100**. Groceries come to about **$300**. This month Jordan also spent **$420** eating out and **$180** on two concerts, and put **$0** into savings.

At the end of the month Jordan opens the bank app and wonders where it all went.

steps.prompt: Add up everything Jordan spent this month.
What was Jordan’s cash flow for the month?
steps.explain: $2,400 − $2,100 = $300. Positive, but none of it was saved on purpose.

steps.prompt: Sort Jordan’s spending.
Jordan wants to save $300 next month without missing rent. Best plan?
choices: Eat out half as often and skip the concerts
Wait and save whatever is left at the end
why: Rent is a need, and missing it can cost you your home.
Groceries are a need. Cut wants first.
That’s exactly what happened this month: $0 saved.
steps.explain: Half the eating out saves $210, skipping the concerts saves $180. That’s $390, more than enough.

steps.context: Planning a month before it starts beats wondering where it went.
steps.prompt: Plan Jordan’s next month. Give every dollar of the $2,400 a job, with at least $300 going to savings.
steps.explain: Any plan works if the needs are covered, savings gets at least $300 and nothing is left without a job.

steps.prompt: If Jordan’s income stays the same, saving more has to come from spending less.
steps.explain: Same money in means the savings come out of what goes out. Wants first.

lessons.title: Your Net Worth
lessons.summary: The one number that keeps score.

steps.context: An [[asset]] is something you own that's worth money: savings in the bank, a car, a laptop you could sell.
steps.prompt: Which of these is an asset?
steps.explain: It's yours and it's worth money. Asset.

steps.context: A [[liability]] is money you owe to someone else, like a loan you're still paying back.
steps.prompt: Which of these is a liability?
choices: A car loan you're paying off
A bike you've fully paid for
steps.explain: You still owe it, so it's a liability.

steps.context: Your [[net worth]] is everything you own minus everything you owe. Own $10,000, owe $4,000, and your net worth is $6,000.
steps.prompt: You have $8,000 in savings and owe $5,000 on a car loan. What’s your net worth?
Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Something you own that's worth money
What you own minus what you owe

steps.prompt: If you earn a lot, your net worth is automatically high.
steps.explain: Earn a lot and spend it all, and you own nothing. Net worth is what you keep.

steps.context: Net worth can drop below zero. If you owe more than you own, it's negative. That's common when you're starting out. What matters is that it grows.
steps.prompt: You own $12,000 and owe $15,000. What’s your net worth? (Use the +/− button for a negative number.)
steps.explain: $12,000 − $15,000 = −$3,000. Now you know the number to beat.

steps.prompt: Which of these raises your net worth?
choices: Taking a new loan to buy a TV
Paying off part of a loan
Spending your savings on a holiday
steps.explain: Owe less, and your net worth goes up.

lessons.title: The Bill Stack
lessons.summary: Read two real bills, catch a charge that shouldn’t be there, pick the cheaper plan.

steps.context: Every bill has a [[due date]]: the last day to pay it without being late.

doc.title: Bright Power
doc.subtitle: Electricity bill
doc.note: Payments received after Oct 21 add a $15.00 late fee.

steps.prompt: What’s the last day you can pay this bill on time?
why: That’s when the billing period ended, not the deadline.
That’s when the billing period started.
steps.explain: The due date is boxed at the top: Oct 21.

doc.title: Bright Power
doc.subtitle: Electricity bill
doc.note: Payments received after Oct 21 add a $15.00 late fee.

steps.prompt: How much do you owe on this bill in total?

steps.context: Pay after the due date and many companies add a [[late fee]]: a penalty for paying late. Read the small print at the bottom.

doc.title: Bright Power
doc.subtitle: Electricity bill
doc.note: Payments received after Oct 21 add a $15.00 late fee.

steps.prompt: You forget, and pay on Oct 25. How much do you pay now?
steps.explain: $84.12 + $15.00 late fee = $99.12. Same electricity, $15 more.

steps.context: Read the lines, not just the total. Mistakes and surprise charges hide in there.
steps.prompt: You didn’t leave the country this month. Which charge shouldn’t be on your phone bill?
steps.explain: Three roaming day passes at $10 each. Call the company and ask them to remove it.

steps.prompt: They agree to take that charge off. What should the new total be?

steps.context: Comparing two prices? Line them up over the same stretch of time, like a full year.
steps.prompt: Over one year, which plan costs less, and by how much?
why: Plan A is $480 a year. Plan B is $410 even with its fee.
That forgets Plan B’s $50 activation fee.
Plan A is $480 a year. Plan B is $410.

steps.prompt: Paying a bill a day after its due date is fine as long as you pay the full amount.
steps.explain: Late is late. You can get a [[late fee]], and repeated late payments can hurt you later.

lessons.title: Maya’s Money Check-Up
lessons.summary: Cash flow and net worth for one real-feeling person.

story.title: A one-page check-up
story.body:
Maya sat down to see where she stands. Each month she takes home **$3,200**. Her expenses: rent **$1,300**, groceries **$350**, a car payment of **$280**, her phone **$60**, and about **$700** on eating out and shopping.

She owns a car worth **$9,000** and has **$2,500** in the bank. She still owes **$6,000** on the car and **$1,200** to a friend.

steps.prompt: Add up Maya’s monthly expenses.
What’s her monthly cash flow?
Add up her assets.
Add up her liabilities.
What’s her net worth?
Need or want?
Maya wants her net worth to grow faster. Best first move?
choices: Trim eating out and shopping, and save the difference
Stop paying what she owes on the car
why: A pricier car usually means more owed, and a car loses value.
Missing payments brings fees and bigger trouble.
steps.explain: Every dollar moved from wants to savings raises her net worth.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you're closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Fundamentals
lessons.summary: Nine questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: You earn more than last year, but your savings haven't grown. Most likely culprit?
steps.explain: Spending quietly rose to match the raise. Classic [[lifestyle creep]].

steps.prompt: You earn $2,800 a month. Rent is $1,100, bills are $600, and food and fun come to $900. What’s your cash flow?
Your net worth can go up even if your income stays the same.
steps.explain: Spend less or pay down what you owe, and it rises. Income isn't the only lever.

steps.prompt: A car loan you're still paying back is a ___.
steps.explain: You owe it, so it's a [[liability]].

steps.prompt: Which move improves your cash flow fastest?
choices: Checking your net worth every day
steps.explain: Less going out means more left over, starting this month.

steps.prompt: This stub doesn’t print the net pay. How much lands in your bank account?
